claims.statement: Captioned viewing generally improves immediate L2 comprehension and/or vocabulary outcomes compared with uncaptioned viewing, but effect magnitude depends on outcome, material and study design.
Lower-proficiency learners can allocate a large share of attention to on-screen captions and rely on written text more than audio during captioned viewing.
Caption reliance varies substantially across individual learners and is related to proficiency/achievement; a one-size caption mode can therefore mismatch learner processing needs.

Full captions are not universally inferior to reduced captions: full captions have outperformed keyword captions for some global-comprehension outcomes, while partial modes can benefit some less-caption-reliant learners.

L1 subtitles can improve immediate content comprehension in some lower-proficiency viewing contexts, while other studies find no subtitle-language effect; L1 versus L2 text effects are task- and population-dependent.
L2 captions provide a direct written representation of the speech stream and can support speech segmentation, form recognition and lexical form-meaning learning.
Repeated viewing can provide additional opportunities for comprehension and form processing, but the resulting attempt is repeated exposure rather than first-seen evidence.
Existing caption-order findings do not justify a universal captions-first or audio-first learning rule; order effects are mixed and can vary with language/script and task outcome.

Progressive reduction from more to less caption support is pedagogically plausible and positively perceived in exploratory work, but direct causal evidence is insufficient for a fixed universal fading sequence.

Captions can continue to improve television content comprehension across a wide proficiency range; a threshold for content comprehension without captions should not be treated as a threshold for listening-skill training without text.

Learners’ viewing-mode preferences and confidence can change with sustained audiovisual exposure, with more proficient learners more likely to shift toward uncaptioned viewing while elementary learners may still prefer L1 support.
Visual and linguistic complexity can increase caption reliance, especially for lower-proficiency learners, so support policy should account for clip complexity rather than proficiency alone.
Because captions and L1 subtitles can provide alternate routes to form or meaning, success while answer-bearing text is visible cannot by itself establish independent listening ability.
The relative pedagogical strength and optimal timing of synchronized captions versus a self-paced full transcript are not established well enough to encode a universal ordering rule.

The optimal adaptive sequence and fading thresholds for replay, L2 form support, Vietnamese micro-gloss, transcript and full L1 meaning support for Vietnamese near-A0 learners require direct product validation.
